title: When Efficiency Becomes a Vulnerability: Computational Cost Attacks on WebAgents
pdf_path: papers/When Efficiency Becomes a Vulnerability_Computational Cost Attacks on WebAgents.pdf
threat_model_summary: A black-box attacker injects content into web pages that induces the agent to consume far more output tokens per task, raising monetary and latency cost. The attacker does not need model weights or tool access; the paper evaluates task-level token cost (TkC) and its increase over benign runs, and does not model an adaptive defender.
core_contributions: CostBomb: a black-box computational cost attack on web agents
An LLM-based injection generator plus a GRPO-trained selector that chooses injection carriers
Two cost metrics, TkC and TkCA, measuring absolute and relative token-cost inflation
Nine SeeAct and three WebVoyager settings with positive Delta-TkC in all nine SeeAct settings
Reports up to Delta-TkC 1.6031 and absolute TkC 24084.03, with a task-success drop from 27.50% to 23.91% in one setting
limitations: Abstract claims no loss of successful task completion, but the only TSR measurement drops by 3.59 pp
TSR is measured in a single SeeAct setting, not across the matrix
Cost accounting counts output tokens only; injected 200-400 character aria-labels also inflate input tokens unmeasured
GRPO ablation is selective: 4 of 12 settings have higher Delta-TkC without GRPO
The entity observing per-task token usage may differ from the page injector, so the threat model subject is unclear
VirusTotal is not a semantic prompt-injection detector; non-detection does not establish invisibility
TkC/AS and TkCA are not mutually derivable in some rows; aggregation is undefined
Single run, no confidence intervals, no code/artifact, no ethics or disclosure section
theoretical_crypto_links: None; no cryptographic definition, security game, construction, theorem, proof, or reduction
The formal-looking generator objective and GRPO loss are optimization, not security definitions
applied_crypto_links: None; no OAuth, TLS, signatures, attestation, TEE, or capability tokens
Cost budgets, rate limits, and signed provenance are our inference; they would bound spend or attribute content, not judge injection semantics
evidence_refs: pp.1-9 threat model, CostBomb, metrics, and main results
pp.13-17 appendices A-D, algorithm, and VirusTotal table

title: Multi-Agent Security Tax: Trading Off Security and Collaboration Capabilities in Multi-Agent Systems
pdf_path: papers/Multi-Agent Security Tax_Trading Off Security and Collaboration Capabilities in Multi-Agent Systems.pdf
threat_model_summary: A seven-agent simulated autonomous chemistry lab is exposed to jailbreak prompts that can induce unsafe collaboration or an explosion. Four prompt/memory interventions (passive/active instructions, passive/active vaccines) are evaluated for robustness and cooperation. There is no formal adversary, adaptive attack, or cryptographic protection.
core_contributions: A seven-agent simulated lab for measuring security and collaboration jointly
A security tax framing: defenses may reduce unsafe behavior but also reduce useful collaboration
Four prompt/memory interventions, including active vaccines delivered through memory
Five-model by five-defense experiments with 36 simulations per condition
A second experiment with 30 histories and 6 conditions on benign anomalous instructions
limitations: The referenced Appendix with system prompts, 12 jailbreaks, vaccine texts, and per-model Figure 3 is absent from the 9-page PDF
Experiment 2 claims 6 models and 5,400 trials but Table 2 lists only 5 rows; column averages do not match the 5 listed rows
Text says a 14-point gain from 76.7% to 90%, which is 13.3 pp
Model naming is inconsistent between text and tables
gpt-3.5-turbo instruction defenses reduce robustness below no defense, unexplained
Abstract says defenses tend to decrease collaboration, but vaccine conditions match or exceed no-defense cooperation
Robustness only measures whether an explosion occurs, not propagation depth or compromise rate
Both outcomes are judged by GPT-4 Omni with no human labels or judge agreement
No significance tests; 36 runs per condition with jailbreak clustering ignored
theoretical_crypto_links: None; no cryptographic primitive, definition, game, theorem, proof, or reduction
Robustness and cooperation are empirical frequencies, not formal security properties
applied_crypto_links: None; no authentication, signing, provenance, or isolation mechanism is used
Tool-level capability and message provenance are our inference; they would constrain action scope, not vaccine semantics
evidence_refs: pp.1-7 protocol, interventions, Tables 1-2, discussion, and limitations
pp.8-9 references browsed only; referenced appendix absent

title: Mind the Third Eye! Benchmarking Privacy Awareness in MLLM-powered Smartphone Agents
pdf_path: papers/Mind the Third Eye! Benchmarking Privacy Awareness in MLLM-powered Smartphone Agents.pdf
threat_model_summary: The benchmark presents privacy-sensitive smartphone instructions and measures whether an MLLM agent recognizes the risk and warns the user. It is a measurement study, not an attack: there is no adversary model, no adaptive attacker, and no enforcement mechanism. Privacy awareness is semantic recognition, not a formal privacy guarantee.
core_contributions: SAPA-Bench: 7,138 scenarios across 50 English apps, 8 categories, 27 subcategories, and 3 sensitivity levels
Two exposure modalities (text and image) and metrics for privacy risk recognition, leakage, and advice
Evaluation of 7 MLLM-based agents showing wide gaps between recognition and safe behavior
Evidence that explicit hints raise risk awareness while no-hint conditions remain low
Analysis of leakage paths and response patterns
limitations: All-positive scenario set makes PRR effectively a recall rate, with no negative controls or false-positive rate
Conditional denominators for PLR/PLAR/PCAR are not comparable
GPT-4o generates reference responses and labels while also being evaluated
Judge model, prompt, and thresholds are only in an absent appendix
No inter-annotator agreement, filtering precision, or rejection rate
Static single-turn scenarios do not test real gating
English apps only; possible GUI corpus contamination
The referenced Appendix with prompt templates, hyperparameters, and RA scoring is absent from the 9-page PDF
Several text/table inconsistencies: Gemini PRR 59.94 vs 55.94, RA 66.14 vs 67.14, GPT-4o 74.42 assigned to the wrong modality
theoretical_crypto_links: None; no cryptographic primitive, definition, theorem, or reduction
Privacy awareness is semantic risk recognition, not differential privacy or cryptographic privacy
applied_crypto_links: None; permission and consent are OS/UI semantics, not verifiable authorization
OAuth, signatures, TEE, or capability tokens are not used or evaluated
evidence_refs: pp.1-7 benchmark construction, metrics, and results
pp.8-9 acknowledgments/references browsed only; referenced appendix absent

title: MobileSafetyBench: Evaluating Safety of Autonomous Agents in Mobile Device Control
pdf_path: papers/MobileSafetyBench_Evaluating Safety of Autonomous Agents in Mobile Device Control.pdf
threat_model_summary: Agents execute 250 mobile tasks, including 50 high-risk daily tasks and 50 high-risk tasks with indirect prompt injection, in an Android emulator. Safety is scored by rule-based evaluators for harmful actions, privacy leakage, and refusal. The threat model is a static injected instruction, not an adaptive attacker.
core_contributions: MobileSafetyBench: 250 tasks over 13 apps, split into low-risk, high-risk, and high-risk IPI
Rule-based safety evaluation covering harmful actions, privacy leakage, and refusal
Evaluation of 10 LLMs plus SeeAct and M3A agents
SCoT prompting mitigation that raises high-risk refusal for GPT-4o from 6% to 36%
Analysis of the gap between task capability and safety refusal
limitations: The referenced Appendices A-F (threat model, evaluator rules, prompts, human survey, app list) are absent from the 9-page PDF
Text says 28% higher but Table 2 shows 6% to 36%, a 30-point gain
GPT-4o SCoT high-risk refusal appears as 31%, 36%, and 41% in different tables/figures
Gemini-1.5 agentic 82% in Table 3 conflicts with about 53% in Figure 3; metric definitions differ
No confidence intervals or multiple seeds
IPI tested on only 3 models with 50 static, simple injections
Phi-4 is a text model compared with multimodal agents, confounding the 3% low-risk success
theoretical_crypto_links: None; no cryptographic primitive, definition, game, theorem, or reduction
The sequential-decision notation is an MDP-style formalism, not a security definition
applied_crypto_links: None; Android permissions and sandboxing are OS access control, not cryptographic capabilities
No signing, attestation, TEE, or verifiable authorization is evaluated
evidence_refs: pp.1-8 benchmark, agents, experiments, and limitations
p.9 references browsed only; referenced appendices absent

title: MCPTox: A Benchmark for Tool Poisoning on Real-World MCP Servers
pdf_path: papers/MCPTox_A Benchmark for Tool Poisoning on Real-World MCP Servers.pdf
threat_model_summary: A malicious MCP server publishes tool descriptions or metadata containing poisoned instructions. The benchmark inserts poisoned tool definitions into the agent system prompt and measures whether the agent follows them. This is prompt-level semantic poisoning, not cryptographic supply-chain tampering, and no live MCP transport or real tool execution is tested.
core_contributions: MCPTox: 1,348 cases over 45 real-world MCP servers and 353 tools
Three poisoning paradigms and ten risk categories
Evaluation of 20 model settings, with average ASR 36.5% and highs of 72.8% for o1-mini
Evidence that stronger models can be more susceptible and refusal rates can be below 3%
Comparison with InjecAgent showing much higher attack success on MCP tool metadata
limitations: Table 1 counts 224+548+725=1,497, conflicting with the 1,348 total
Prompt-level simulation inserts poisoned tools into the system prompt; no live MCP transport or execution
20 agents are 20 model settings on one pipeline, not 20 distinct agent architectures
No clean baseline, utility measurement, defense experiment, or adaptive attack
No model versions, temperatures, repetitions, or confidence intervals
Abstract says 10 risk categories while the body says 11
P1 average 36.7 is not reproducible from its rows and appears to be a misplaced value
27.8% applies only to Qwen3-8b; Claude-3.7-sonnet anomaly is unexplained
Only metadata sanitization, sandboxing, and auditing are suggested, none implemented or measured
theoretical_crypto_links: None; no cryptographic primitive, definition, theorem, proof, or reduction
Poisoning is semantic manipulation of tool descriptions, not cryptographic integrity compromise
applied_crypto_links: None; the paper does not evaluate signing, provenance, allowlists, or attested MCP servers
Signed tool manifests and registry transparency are our inference; they would authenticate publisher identity, not the safety of tool semantics
evidence_refs: pp.1-8 benchmark construction, paradigms, results, and limitations
p.9 references browsed only; no appendix exists
